article.articleSummary:

article.articleHeadline: Surveillance Failures Caused Rapid Spread of Ebola in Ituri - Taarifa Rwanda:
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-09-13, Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with Ituri as the hardest-hit province, reached more than 6,800 confirmed cases and over 3,300 deaths nationally, and over 5,400 cases in Ituri alone. National Deputy Iracan Gratien de Saint-Nicolas, speaking in Bunia, blamed rapid spread on failures in epidemiological surveillance and weak early detection, criticizing the system's reporting chain from health areas to the ministry. He called for accountability and for lessons to be learned, noting structural weaknesses and the need for permanent isolation facilities in hospitals rather than ad hoc setups during epidemics. He suggested the virus might have circulated before first detection, possibly as early as January or February, though further research is needed to pin down the timeline. Kinshasa government says the Ebola epidemic has been brought under control.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Ituri: Professor Muyembe urges turning experience into results.
article.articleSummary: Ebola in Ituri, North-East Democratic Republic of the Congo, saw Professor Jean-Jacques Muyembe urge turning the DRC’s Ebola response experience into concrete results. After visiting the Ituri provincial laboratory in Bunia, he noted that the President places trust in the country and the world watches, stressing the need to demonstrate on the ground the Republic’s extensive Ebola expertise. During his mission, Muyembe met the outbreak response coordination, the World Health Organization, care and research teams, and staff of the Ituri Provincial Public Health Laboratory. He said response effectiveness depends on all actors working in a unified direction and fully embracing their responsibilities, transcending institutional lines. The remarks were conveyed through an INRB press release cited by ACP. The call reinforces leveraging coordinated, cross-institutional effort to end the Ebola outbreak.

This suggests a favorable evolution of the epidemiological situation, but ongoing surveillance is required to quickly identify any suspected case. article.articleHeadline: The US Is Paying to Keep Ebola Patients Out of America, While Cutting the Programs That Stop Outbreaks at the Source
article.articleSummary: Outbreak: Ebola in Central Africa expanded in 2026; US strategy prioritized preventing infected or exposed travelers from reaching U.S. shores, including a Kenya-built, 50-bed bio-isolation unit for asymptomatic Americans exposed in Congo or Uganda. By May, Washington imposed travel restrictions and expanded airport screening; CDC reported four U.S. airports conducting screening, over 230 staff engaged, and an emergency fund of $107 million activated on June 18 for domestic and international response. Do-not-board orders required Congo travelers to complete 21 days in a third country before flying home. Reuters noted 14 American citizens were quarantined at a New York military base for four days after Congo return. Public accounting of monitored travelers and activated hospitals remained unclear. CDC asserts stopping Ebola at its source with Congo/Uganda offices. Critics argue USAID cuts and firing thousands of CDC staff reduced preparedness; Washington funds containment abroad while restricting entry domestically.

article.articleHeadline: Mpox vs Covid: Why Clade Ib is different and how concerned should India be?
article.articleSummary: Mpox Clade Ib spreads mainly through direct physical contact and contaminated materials; not airborne as COVID-19, so the general population risk remains low despite wider geographic spread. Clade Ib, a subclade of Clade I first identified in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2023, has drawn attention for community transmission beyond established areas. Mpox transmission occurs via close contact, including sexual contact and exposure to body fluids; rare aerosol transmission is possible during prolonged talking but not considered airborne in everyday settings. Incubation is typically 1–21 days; symptoms resemble smallpox with fever, headache, fatigue, muscle pain, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, followed by a deep, painful rash with central depressions that crust. Vulnerable groups include those with severely suppressed immunity, pregnant women, and children; healthcare workers and household contacts are at higher infection risk. India should not panic, as WHO deems the risk low, though surveillance and vaccination discussions continue.

article.articleHeadline: In the DRC, doctors are facing difficulties in the fight against the Ebola outbreak.
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease is spreading in Ituri province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where residents impede medical teams from examining bodies of deceased patients showing symptoms. Investigators cannot access 42 corpses due to resistance from relatives, hindering lab confirmation and tissue sampling needed to determine Ebola infection and to map transmission chains. The lack of verified data makes it difficult to assess the outbreak’s true scale in the eastern DRC and to understand death-cause patterns and infection routes. For the period August 26–September 1, the DRC recorded 295 deaths, with 210 occurring in communities and 85 in medical facilities. Ongoing data gaps delay focused public health responses and contact-tracing efforts essential to interrupt transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Tiny RNA Molecule Pushes Schistosome Parasites Toward Self-Destruction
article.articleSummary: Schistosoma japonicum, a major cause of human and animal schistosomiasis in Asia, may be steered toward apoptosis by a single microRNA, sja-miR-2a-3p. In permissive BALB/c mice, parasites flourish; in less-permissive Wistar rats they exhibit higher apoptotic activity. Expression of sja-miR-2a-3p is elevated during 14–28 days post-infection, especially in schistosomula from Wistar rats, with tissue enrichment in the male testis and posterior region and in the female vitellaria. Computational targets include several apoptosis-related genes; functional tests in vitro showed that mimics or inhibitors of sja-miR-2a-3p modulate apoptosis gene transcripts and egg output, with TUNEL staining confirming DNA fragmentation. Findings link host environment, parasite apoptosis, and a regulatory RNA, hinting at new control strategies that disrupt parasite survival by targeting its own gene regulation. Acta Parasitologica; authors Sun and Zhong; Shanxi Agricultural University and Shanghai Veterinary Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences.

article.articleHeadline: An 80-year-old man contracts tetanus after a branch scratch; doctors say it's not just rusty nails that can cause tetanus—these situations can also lead to tetanus.
article.articleSummary: China faces tetanus from minor wounds; an 80-year-old Beijing woman developed tetanus after a branch scratch, and earlier a 70-something patient contracted tetanus from a chicken-peck wound at home. These cases show rusty nails are not required. Clostridium tetani, common in soil, animal feces, and dust, forms spores that germinate in anaerobic wounds. Symptoms include mouth-opening difficulty, lockjaw, a sardonic smile, and back muscle stiffness; generalized spasms and autonomic changes such as high blood pressure and rapid heart rate; in the elderly, arrhythmias and heart failure are possible. Case fatality can reach about 10%. Seek prompt care for deep, narrow wounds to decide on tetanus antitoxin or immune globulin. Vaccination offers protection for 5–10 years; outdoor workers should stay up to date. Beijing Ditan Hospital’s Pu Lin stresses vaccination and early treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Knowledge Nugget | Foot and Mouth Disease: What is SAT-1 and why is its return matter of concern
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) SAT-1, a serotype traditionally linked to southern Africa, has reappeared in Europe and the Middle East after about six decades. SAT-1 was first identified in 1948; WOAH reports 2025 detections in Iraq, Kuwait, Egypt, and Azerbaijan, with 2026 additions in Israel, Cyprus, Palestine, China and Mongolia. Türkiye, Lebanon and Greece also reported the serotype again after ~60 years. FMD is a highly contagious viral disease affecting cloven-hoofed livestock (cattle, buffaloes, pigs, sheep, goats); signs include fever, blisters in the mouth and on feet, lameness, reduced milk yield. There is no specific antiviral treatment; control relies on vaccination and biosecurity. In India, the NADCP (launched 2019; under LHDCP since 2021) supports large-scale vaccination, vaccine procurement, cold-chain strengthening, and awareness for FMD and Brucellosis control. Human health risk is minimal, though the economic impact includes trade embargo risks and livestock losses.

article.articleHeadline: Discovery of a virus that threatens vision... what is its connection to seafood?
article.articleSummary: CMNV, a virus known to infect aquatic animals, is linked to a human emergent anterior ocular disease POH-VAU, causing recurrent inflammation and sustained elevated intraocular pressure that risks optic nerve damage and vision loss if not diagnosed and treated early. A Nature study by collaborators from China, Australia, and Singapore analyzed 70 patients with this eye condition, finding viral infection signatures in ocular tissues and immune indicators consistent with CMNV exposure. Transmission is most often via direct contact with aquatic animals during seafood cleaning/processing or consumption of raw seafood, together accounting for about 71.4% of cases; increased exposure intensity correlates with higher risk. Preventive measures include gloves and protective gear when handling seafood, thorough handwashing, and avoiding undercooked products. Prompt ophthalmology consultation is advised for redness, pain, blurred vision, or recurrent inflammation to mitigate serious complications.

article.articleHeadline: In August, Guangdong saw sharp declines in COVID-19, influenza, and hand, foot, and mouth disease cases.
article.articleSummary: Guangdong Province reports declines in COVID-19, influenza, and hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) for August 2026. From August 1–31, 35,782 new COVID-19 infections were reported with no deaths, down 49.9% from July. Influenza reached 233,996 cases with 1 death, down 45.6%; HFMD 19,494 cases, down 64.8%. Overall, 351,809 statutory infectious disease cases were reported in August, with 119 deaths; Class A recorded no cases or deaths. Class B had 75,617 cases and 118 deaths; the top five were COVID-19, hepatitis B, syphilis, tuberculosis, and gonorrhea, accounting for 94.81% of Class B. Class C reported 276,192 cases and 1 death; the top three were influenza, other infectious diarrhoeal diseases, and HFMD, making up 99.72% of Class C. Several diseases such as visceral leishmaniasis, echinococcosis, and filariasis had no reported cases or deaths.

article.articleHeadline: In Guangzhou, a woman spotted a giant snail in a green belt; its shell is larger than an adult man's fist; experts warn: do not touch or eat it, as its parasite can cause meningitis.
article.articleSummary: Giant African snail spotted in Guangzhou; shell larger than a fist. Achatina fulica, an invasive species introduced from Africa to China in the 1930s, is a major pest. In Guangdong (Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Jiangmen) infection rates of Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm) in these snails range 27%-41%, with each carrying more than 150 parasites. Humans acquire meningitis from the parasite via eating raw or undercooked snail meat, contact with contaminated produce, or exposure to snail slime or feces. The snail also harbors bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Salmonella, E. coli, and Listeria. It reproduces rapidly (30-700 eggs). Guidance: do not touch or eat; wash produce; if contact occurs, wash with soap for 3 minutes and disinfect wounds; seek care if fever, headache, vomiting, or rash within 72 hours. Disposal: wear gloves, move snail with tongs into lime/salt container, seal and discard; keep damp areas dry for 48 hours.

article.articleHeadline: BRICS countries will create a system to respond to infectious disease outbreaks.
article.articleSummary: BRICS nations agreed to create an integrated BRICS system to respond to infectious disease outbreaks and to issue early warnings, announced by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the BRICS+ summit in New Delhi. The plan aims to coordinate rapid response, surveillance, and information sharing across BRICS and BRICS+ partners. The backdrop includes the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which the World Health Organization reported as causing 796 deaths; on May 17, WHO declared the Congo–Uganda Ebola situation an emergency and a threat to other countries. The New Delhi summit coincided with leaders such as Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping, Cyril Ramaphosa, and Abiy Ahmed, and produced a declaration opposing unilateral sanctions. BRICS accounts for roughly 40% of world GDP and nearly half of the global population.

article.articleHeadline: Officials launch door-to-door mosquito alert after ovitrap index hits 64%
article.articleSummary: Macau recorded an ovitrap index of 63.9% in August, signaling elevated risk of mosquito-borne disease transmission. Health officials launched a door-to-door alert, targeting 30,000 residences, as part of a twice-yearly citywide effort to eliminate stagnant water; this campaign was expanded to districts with higher mosquito indices, dense populations, larger elderly populations, and concentrations of low-rise buildings. Intelligent bio-mosquito traps from the mainland are being tested at hospitals and other sites; deployment density and effectiveness are under evaluation. Officials stress an integrated approach with source reduction as the top priority; traps may supplement measures if crowding keeps numbers high in public areas. Residents are urged to clear stagnant water, install window screens, and use outdoor mosquito repellent; Macau hosts 200+ public locations offering shared repellent. Aedes albopictus carries dengue and chikungunya.

article.articleHeadline: Jointly Building a Harmonious and Safe Homeland: Mianyang Launches Rabies Prevention and Control Pilot Program
article.articleSummary: Rabies prevention and control pilot, 'Dog Wind-Chime – Dog Immunization, Human Safety', launched in Jiangyou, Mianyang, Sichuan. Led by the Mianyang Bureau of Agriculture and Rural Affairs and the Animal Epidemic Prevention and Control Center, and hosted by Jiangyou Agriculture and Rural Affairs Bureau, the event inaugurates a province-wide pilot in Mianyang. The program targets source control and proactive prevention. Jiangyou designated 7 pet clinics as 'Animal Rabies Immunization Points' and established 13 rural 'Immunization Service Teams', forming an urban fixed vaccination and rural mobile immunization network for dogs. A civil dog-ownership pledge was issued; services included vaccination, veterinary exams, provision of dog-raising supplies, rabies prevention education, dog-bite emergency guidance, and related inquiries. In 2026, the provincial center continues the 'Dog Wind-Chime' pilot; Jiangyou is one of three pilot sites. Ongoing work covers dog population surveys, centralized immunization, and routine public awareness to sustain dog vaccination and human–dog harmony.

No clinical details or case breakdown are provided. It remains a social-media aggregation rather than a public-health briefing. article.articleHeadline: Screening Nearly 150,000 Migrants Reveals Hidden Tuberculosis Burden in the
article.articleSummary: Five-year national TB screening in the Netherlands (2019–2023) analyzed 149,214 migrants to map active TB and latent infection in a low-incidence setting. Immigrants (87,511) yielded 69 TB cases (79/100k); asylum seekers (61,703) yielded 170 cases (276/100k). Country-level yields exceeded birth-country WHO incidence for asylum seekers, with Sierra Leone (888), Eritrea (704), Somalia (581), Gambia (562) and South Sudan/Sudan (519) top; immigrants’ highest yields were Indonesia (291) and the Philippines (241). Symptom-based detection was weak: of 202 screen-detected pulmonary TB cases, 27.2% reported cough (immigrants 13.8%, asylum seekers 32.6%). About 56.5% of 239 screen-detected TB cases were bacteriologically confirmed; two MDR-TB cases. Treatment outcomes: immigrants 92.8% cured/completed vs asylum seekers 81.2%, with loss to follow-up and cross-border movement driving the gap. A second component analyzed latent infection in >20,000 immigrants, rising with age (0.6% under 12, 4.4% among adolescent). Implications for Europe include radiological screening value and cross-border care continuity.

article.articleHeadline: Papua Highlands Provincial Government pushes for a four-step approach to managing Acute Mountain Sickness.
article.articleSummary: Papua Highlands Provincial Government, via the local Health Department, pushes a four-step strategy to tackle AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria (ATM) across six districts: Jayawijaya, Mamberamo Tengah, Nduga, Pegunungan Bintang, Yalimo, and Yahukimo. In Wamena, Isak Yando stated the plan: (1) data-driven policy using real-time surveillance to target interventions; (2) cross-sector integration to coordinate efforts; (3) strengthening the Papua Highlands Partnership Forum among government, partners, academia, business, and civil society; (4) concrete regional actions in the six lokus. Programs must be embedded in RPJMD, RKPD, and APBD to ensure sustained funding. The strategy emphasizes integrated ATM prevention and control, with district-level action plans to be developed and implemented to achieve effective outcomes.

article.articleSummary: Surabaya's Health Office reports a slight uptick in fever and influenza cases amid recent weather changes, though numbers remain within normal range. Rumors that Surabaya hospitals are full due to influenza type A are unfounded; services at hospitals and puskesmas remain normal. Inpatients are those requiring further medical management, such as severe respiratory distress; most fever or influenza cases are treated on an outpatient basis. The office emphasizes hospital preparedness, continuous coordination with hospitals and clinics to monitor bed occupancy and staff, and advises seeking care at the nearest puskesmas for complaints while avoiding unverified information.

article.articleHeadline: UNJA Niraga Tea: Antioxidant and Dengue Antiviral Innovation
article.articleSummary: UNJA student team from Universitas Jambi has secured 2026 PKM-RE funding from Dirjen Dikti. The five-member, cross-disciplinary group—led by Muhammad Faris Rizqullah (Medicine, 2023) and including Nurul Fathiah Azzahra (Medicine, 2023), Anjeli Bismi Arsy (Biology, 2024), Kireina Nurfadhillah (Medicine, 2024), and Arum Kinasih Ramadhani (Pharmacy, 2024)—will develop Teh Niraga, a polyherbal tea from corn silk and red onion skin waste, combined with Phyllanthus niruri (meniran) and stevia. It targets antioxidant activity and dengue virus antiviral properties. In vitro assays and in silico simulations will assess molecular interactions with dengue proteins. The team aims to reduce dengue burden in Indonesia, including Jambi, and advance toward data generation for potential participation in PIMNAS in October 2026.

article.articleHeadline: E. coli in MBG's Turmeric-Spiced Chicken Triggers Food Poisoning Among 161 Students in Toraja
article.articleSummary: E. coli contamination in yellow-spiced chicken served under the Free Nutritious Meals (MBG) program sparked a food-poisoning outbreak among 161 students in Makale, Tana Toraja, South Sulawesi, Indonesia. The affected pupils attend SMPN 1/2 Makale and SDN 5/9 Tana Toraja, with gastrointestinal symptoms including diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. BBPOM Makassar laboratory results confirmed Escherichia coli in the yellow chicken samples: 5.7 × 10^3 CFU/g for samples consumed by middle-school students and 5.3 × 10^3 CFU/g for those consumed by elementary students. Other MBG foods (white rice, tempe mendoan, vegetables, tilapia) tested negative for microbiological hazards and chemical contaminants; melon samples were negative for major pathogens but contained trace nitrite, likely naturally occurring. Dinas Kesehatan Toraja cites these findings as part of tracing the outbreak source. The report is dated 14 September 2026.

article.articleHeadline: India's 2026 H1N1 Surge Driven by Known Seasonal Strain
article.articleSummary: Delhi-National Capital Region faces a 2026 influenza A(H1N1) surge driven by an established A(H1N1)pdm09 lineage, specifically the A/Missouri/11/2025(H1N1)pdm09-like variant, per Indian Council of Medical Research surveillance and New Microbes and New Infections analysis. The surge stems from a familiar strain, enabling use of existing vaccines and antivirals rather than a novel reassortant. The virus, an Orthomyxoviridae member with a negative-sense segmented RNA genome, relies on hemagglutinin for receptor binding and neuraminidase for virion release. Transmission in Delhi NCR is shaped by high humidity, monsoon, winter inversions, indoor crowding, aerosols, and fomites, with a 1–4 day incubation and presymptomatic shedding. Clinically, A(H1N1) ranges from mild upper respiratory illness to severe pneumonia and ARDS, with bacterial superinfections by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pyogenes worsening outcomes. High-risk groups include pregnant women and infants under five.

article.articleHeadline: Hepatitis A Immunity Stays High in Urban India While Hepatitis E Exposure
article.articleSummary: In urban Vellore, southern India, IgG serology for hepatitis A virus (HAV) and hepatitis E virus (HEV) was measured in two cross-sectional cohorts (2013: n=600; 2022: n=558), ages 1–40. HAV immunity remained highly endemic and uniform across years: seroprevalence >80% among 1–5-year-olds and 100% by age 16+, with no statistically significant year-to-year differences. HEV exposure stayed low in youth and increased gradually with age; among adults 26–40, seroprevalence rose from 18% (2013) to 24% (2022), a non-significant change. Cluster analyses showed HAV seroprevalence was uniformly high across neighborhoods, while HEV exposure was low and heterogeneous, indicating localized risk factors. The estimated effective reproduction number for HAV (Re) was below 1 in both surveys, implying no sustained secondary transmission. Findings reflect a stable HAV-endemic milieu amid urban development and a patchy, slowly accumulating HEV exposure, with surveillance implications.

article.articleHeadline: Climate change, waterlogging fuel vector-borne disease risk in NE: Parliament panel
article.articleSummary: As of 13 September 2026, a Parliament Standing Committee report on vector-borne diseases in North East India warns that the North Eastern Region (NER)’s unique geo-climatic, ecological, and socio-economic setting yields high receptivity and perennial transmission of vector-borne diseases (VBDs). Key determinants include environmental and climatic conditions, abundant water bodies, deforestation, shifting cultivation, and unplanned urbanisation. Intense monsoon rains create ideal mosquito breeding habitats, while paddy fields, ponds, blocked drains, and poorly maintained water storage systems boost proliferation. Dense forest cover supports forest-dwelling vectors such as Anopheles dirus and Anopheles fluviatilis, described as highly efficient malaria vectors. The report underscores elevated vulnerability to VBDs in NE India, though no specific case counts or outbreaks are cited in the article.

article.articleHeadline: From pandemics to supply shocks, PM Modi pushes crisis-ready BRICS; bloc agrees on disease early-warning system
article.articleSummary: At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, BRICS leaders approved an integrated Early Warning System for infectious diseases and Data Integration Guidelines for disaster management, advancing Modi’s four-pillar agenda: resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. The commitments were welcomed by WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, who highlighted universal health coverage, resilient health systems, tuberculosis, the health workforce, digital health and traditional medicine within the New Delhi Declaration’s health framework. UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged peace from Gaza and the broader Middle East to Ukraine and Sudan, urging adherence to the UN Charter and international law. The New Delhi Declaration expressed grave concern over Middle East tensions, called for maximum restraint, a Gaza ceasefire and an immediate permanent ceasefire in Sudan, and reaffirmed WHO’s coordinating role. The summit framed pandemics, climate disasters and supply-chain disruptions as interconnected, cross-border risks requiring proactive preparedness.

article.articleHeadline: Jyolikot jaundice outbreak: 471 screened, samples for 50 people; five new patients admitted.

article.articleHeadline: Outbreak of Lumpy Skin Disease in Haryana; More Than 150 Cows Dead; Questions for the Department of Animal Husbandry

Officials say 1.461 million animals have been vaccinated, but farmers question vaccine effectiveness and coverage. Transmission is via insects (mosquitoes, flies) and direct contact, contaminated feed, or movement of infected cattle, including imports from Rajasthan, with no curbs on movement yet. Preventive measures include farm sanitation, insect control, nets, neem smoke; isolation of ill animals; treatment emphasizes nutrition and boosting immunity with tulsi, black pepper, turmeric, giloy, jaggery decoctions, neem-water baths, and topical coconut oil.

article.articleHeadline: Livestock owners, beware! A dangerous disease silently spreading from animals to humans.
article.articleSummary: Brucellosis, a bacterial zoonosis, poses a risk to livestock workers in India, especially those caring for cows, buffaloes, and goats. Infected animals can silently transmit the disease to humans, with abortion-related materials (placenta and discharges) identified as key exposure sources. Humans can contract via contact with contaminated wounds or eyes, and through consuming raw or inadequately heated milk or dairy products. Symptoms include fever, extreme fatigue, headaches, and muscle and joint pains; fever can be prolonged. At Karauli MCH Hospital, General Medicine specialist Dr. Shailendra Gupta confirms Brucellosis is caused by Brucella and primarily affects animals but can spread to people. Senior veterinarian Dr. Brahm Pande notes that post-abortion placenta and discharges are significant infection sources, and exposure via skin lesions or eye contact increases risk. Preventive guidance: boil milk before consumption and avoid touching contaminated material with bare hands; seek veterinary advice if exposure is suspected.

article.articleHeadline: How Bhutan eliminated dog-transmitted human rabies -- and what India can learn
article.articleSummary: Bhutan has eliminated dog-transmitted human rabies as a public-health problem, becoming the first country in WHO's South-East Asia Region to achieve this milestone. WHO validated the achievement on September 4, 2026, after confirming no human deaths from dog-mediated rabies since June 2023. The elimination was driven by sustained vaccination, dog sterilisation, surveillance, and free treatment for bite victims. India has the same tools and a 2030 deadline, but rising dog bites, unreliable data, and uneven local implementation have hindered progress toward the milestone. This Bhutan achievement underscores the impact of coordinated vaccination, sterilisation, surveillance, and accessible treatment in interrupting dog-mediated rabies transmission at the national level.

Expedited review attempts followed: broker Yang Mo pressed candidate Kim Seung-won for swift approval, and Kim, then Justice Minister nominee, allegedly asked MFDS officials to monitor GenenCell favorably; Phase 2 approval occurred on Oct 26, 2021. A 1st‑court ruling found Professor Kang Mo violated pharmaceutical law by directing deletion of the unfavorable hamster data. Separate allegations included a 32 billion won government grant-skimming and 5 billion won stock manipulation. article.articleHeadline: Why is the antigen kit positive but ELISA negative? A big discrepancy in dengue reports between Bhagalpur's JLNMCH and private labs - Bhagalpur dengue test discrepancy: private vs JLNMCH reports.
article.articleSummary: As of 14 September 2026, seven dengue patients in Bhagalpur were admitted to JLNMCH after private labs reported dengue-positive results, but subsequent government ELISA tests at the hospital were negative, and all seven were discharged. The discrepancy arises because private labs commonly use antigen rapid card kits and CBC, which can flag dengue if platelet counts fall—even though CBC is not a definitive confirmatory test. Government standards consider ELISA as the most authentic diagnostic method. Experts note delayed hospital presentation: patients often seek private testing after 3–4 days of illness and reach the hospital after 5–7 days, by which time the virus in blood wanes and antibodies rise, yielding negative ELISA results. Symptoms include high fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, muscle/joint pain, vomiting, and poor appetite. Clinicians advise early ELISA testing within 2–3 days of symptom onset for timely, accurate diagnosis and treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Find out what the West Nile virus is, which caused 41 deaths in Italy and has already reached Brazil - Jornal O Sul
article.articleSummary: West Nile virus infections are reported in Italy and Brazil in 2026. Italy has 41 deaths and 594 confirmed cases through September 8, per the ISS weekly bulletin. In Brazil, four confirmed cases in 2026 with one death, affecting São Paulo and Santa Catarina. West Nile virus is a flavivirus first identified in Uganda in 1937 and now circulating across multiple regions. It is transmitted mainly by Culex mosquitoes; birds, especially migratory species, are natural reservoirs. Most infections are asymptomatic; about 20% develop mild illness with abrupt fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, headache, myalgias, rash, and lymphadenopathy. A small proportion progress to neuroinvasive disease (meningitis, encephalitis, paralysis). No antiviral or human vaccine exists; management is supportive, with hospitalization or ICU as needed. Prevention includes repellents, screens, eliminating standing water, sanitation, and avoiding handling dead animals.

article.articleHeadline: Maceió warns of low uptake of the BCG vaccine and reinforces protection against severe forms of tuberculosis.
article.articleSummary: Maceió, Brazil, warns of low uptake of the BCG vaccine and reinforces protection against severe tuberculosis forms. The free, safe BCG vaccine is targeted at children living within 1 km of confirmed TB cases as part of a focused immunization effort. Routine BCG is indicated from birth and can be given up to age 5, with a single-dose schedule funded by the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS). Although BCG does not fully prevent infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, it substantially reduces the risk of severe disease such as miliary tuberculosis and tuberculous meningitis in young children. Availability is through public health units; parents are urged to consult the nearest service to verify vaccine access and keep vaccination records updated. The campaign emphasizes vaccination as a key strategy to prevent disease and reduce TB‑related hospitalizations and deaths.

article.articleHeadline: Electronic tongue detects avian influenza in six minutes.
article.articleSummary: Six-minute detection of antibodies against H5N1 avian influenza achieved by a multichannel electronic tongue developed at the University of São Carlos (USP) Institute of Physics (IFSC). The platform uses renewable-protein coatings—zein from corn, jacalin from jackfruit, and concanavalin A from beans—to modify gold nanoparticles, forming four sensors that generate an electrical fingerprint when antibodies bind to H5N1. Coupled with machine learning, it differentiates H5N1-positive samples from healthy and other avian diseases with 98.6% accuracy. The device targets clinical and veterinary contexts, enabling rapid surveillance to map regions and species exposure and aid early containment of outbreaks. Although promising, calibration sensitivity and sensor wear pose challenges for commercialization. The approach offers a low-cost, rapid alternative for detecting avian influenza antibodies and could be adapted to other viral targets.

article.articleHeadline: Memorial in Porto Alegre brings to light the history of the first hospital in Rio Grande do Sul to fight tuberculosis.
article.articleSummary: Porto Alegre, Rio Grande do Sul, will inaugurate the Belém Sanatorium Memorial on Sept 17, 2026, at Casa da Memória Unimed Federação/RS, preserving the state’s first hospital devoted to tuberculosis. The Belém Sanatorium began admitting patients on May 15, 1940, with an official opening on Oct 12, 1943, in a ceremony led by Getúlio Vargas. Conceived as one of South America’s most modern TB facilities, it spurred the region’s tisiology network, giving rise to the Sanatório Partenon (1951) and the Pavilhão Pereira Filho (1965). After public-health policy shifts in the 1970s, it became Hospital Parque Belém in 1975, continuing service until operations ceased in May 2017. The memorial assembles images, videos, early 20th‑century theses, medical equipment, and rare books—such as the institution’s Golden Book—curated by José Francisco Alves and Salus Loch, with support from Nilson Luiz May and Luiz Augusto Pereira.

The CCZ conducted 1,198 leishmaniasis tests and 27 sporotrichosis exams, and collected 27 animals with suspected zoonoses found in public spaces. It also collected 4,000 scorpions for monitoring and prevention of accidents and health risks to residents. The activities form part of ongoing surveillance, monitoring of animals and vectors, and disease prevention, aiming to identify focal points and reduce disease circulation in the municipality. The report underscores the CCZ's role in public health protection through diagnostic testing, vector surveillance, and response to animal incidents in public areas. Source: Jornal Panorama via Prefeitura de Pará de Minas.

article.articleHeadline: São Bernardo expands vaccination and maintains zero-dose against measles.
article.articleSummary: São Bernardo do Campo, in the Greater ABC region of São Paulo, Brazil, reports vaccination expansion with 690,436 doses administered Jan–Aug 2026, up from 636,734 in the same period in 2024 (8.4% rise). The municipality has the highest newborn vaccine coverage in the region and leads in 12 of 16 vaccines for under-1-year-olds. Immunization Director Jéssica de Cássia Santos Soares attributes gains to intensified extramural outreach and regular vaccinator training. Measles measures include a zero-dose for infants 6–11 months (launched July after local cases) and an indiscriminate vaccination campaign for 6 months to 59 years from Aug 3 to Sep 1, which yielded over 217,000 doses and coincided with no new cases. Post-campaign, vaccines remain at UBSs per the National Vaccination Schedule; two additional vaccination points will operate on Sep 26 (Regina Rocco Casa I, Vila São Pedro; Luiz Gushiken, Alves Dias).

article.articleHeadline: Cataguases vaccinates 65 heifers against brucellosis in the Cataguarino district.
article.articleSummary: 65 heifers aged 3-8 months were vaccinated against bovine brucellosis in Cataguases' Cataguarino district last week by the Municipal Secretariat of Agriculture and Environment (SAMA). This immunization is part of ongoing preventive and sanitary-control efforts to protect the municipality’s herd from brucellosis, an infectious disease that can cause abortions and infertility in cattle. Brucellosis is a zoonosis, so measures also aim to prevent transmission to humans. The vaccination followed sanitary norms, and the municipality targets about 1,000 animals protected per year in Cataguases, with the 65-dose action contributing to that goal. The initiative underscores coordinated efforts to safeguard animal and public health by reducing brucellosis risk in the region.

article.articleHeadline: Azithromycin Resistance in Gonorrhea Shifts Genetic Ground, Challenging
article.articleSummary: Azithromycin resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae is rising globally, undermining ceftriaxone-azithromycin dual therapy for uncomplicated gonorrhea. WHO classifies this pathogen as high-priority due to rapid resistance evolution and few new drugs in development; ceftriaxone 1 g IM remains first-line, while zoliflodacin and gepotidacin offer limited alternatives. Strains with concurrent ceftriaxone and azithromycin resistance have emerged in several regions, and high treatment costs hinder access in resource-limited settings. In 2022, azithromycin resistance was detected in 46 of 53 countries (87%), with ≥5% resistance in 36 countries. European data (2020–2022) show resistance at 9.4% (up from 8.0% in 2018). In the US, elevated-MIC isolates rose to 4.6% in 2018 and 5.9% in 2019. In the Western Pacific, China reached 16.9% in 2022, while the Philippines remained susceptible.

article.articleHeadline: Albay under state of emergency due to rise in dengue cases
article.articleSummary: Albay province in the Philippines declared a state of emergency over a dengue surge. Public elementary and high schools will suspend classes Monday–Friday next week; private schools will suspend Thursday–Friday. A province-wide 'search and destroy' campaign targets 720 barangays including schools, on Thursday, with one fogging machine provided to each of 15 municipalities. A 'food for work' program supports livelihoods affected. All government hospitals are on red alert for dengue patients. Executive Order No. 51, Series 2026 reactivates ABKD and barangay dengue brigades to mobilize officials, health workers, volunteers, schools, establishments, civil society, and residents. APHO reports 1,457 dengue cases Jan 1–Sep 2 with 11 deaths, up 27.37% from 1,144 cases and 3 deaths in the same period 2025. State of emergency enables use of disaster and health funds for emergency procurement and public health actions.

article.articleHeadline: ASF puts Isabela hog raisers' livelihoods at risk
article.articleSummary: African swine fever (ASF) is spreading in Isabela, Philippines, threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of hog raisers. The outbreak has reached 18 towns and 85 villages, already affecting 120 raisers across Isabela. Provincial authorities have intensified containment with 24/7 quarantine checkpoints at entry and exit points and immediate laboratory examination of suspected cases at the Animal Disease Diagnostics Laboratory. AVAC ASF LIVE vaccines are being administered to eligible fatteners and piglets, while disinfectants are distributed to LGUs, along with flame disinfection and intensified field monitoring and information campaigns. Hog raisers are urged to tighten biosecurity: restrict movement of people, animals, feeds, equipment, and other materials; promptly report sick or unusually dying pigs; and avoid moving, selling, or slaughtering suspected infected animals. Governor Rodolfo T. Albano III appeals for public cooperation to protect Isabela's hog industry and prevent further livelihood losses.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue strikes!
article.articleSummary: Dengue strikes in the Philippines, with a dengue outbreak declared in Bohol after Aug 26 as cases reach epidemic thresholds and mortalities are reported. A Cebu-based critical-care clinician recounts a fatal dengue case: a patient arrived in shock with bleeding needing transfusion, but blood products were unavailable, and she died within 12 hours. The Dengue Integrated Program (DIP) of the PPSCV continues to train health-care workers through caravans and seminars, including a workshop at Governor Celestino Gallares Memorial Medical Center in Bohol. Incidence is reportedly lower than the same period last year, but officials caution against complacency in this endemic country aiming for WHO’s 2030 zero-death target. Recommendations emphasize early testing, avoiding aspirin, maintaining rehydration with oral salts, encouraging blood donors, and considering the newer-generation dengue vaccine now licensed in other endemic nations. Dengue can be fatal.

Many patients are severe, featuring high fever, migraines, and intense muscle pains. Bangkok confirms another epidemiological wave affecting the country. The outbreak is spilling over to travelers, including Russian tourists and remote workers, who report vacations disrupted by nighttime fevers and heavy sweating. Officials urge avoiding large crowds, maintaining mask use in indoor spaces, and close self-monitoring of symptoms. article.articleHeadline: When should a child with Influenza A be taken to a healthcare facility?
article.articleSummary: Influenza A in children is often mild but can progress to severe illness—respiratory failure, pneumonia, hypoxia, meningitis, myocarditis, and secondary bacterial infections—potentially life-threatening. Risk is higher in children under 2 and those with chronic heart, lung, or kidney disease, metabolic disorders, anemia, or immunodeficiency. At home, monitor closely and seek care for red flags: fever ≥39°C not easing; fever lasting >3 days or worsening; seizures; lethargy or confusion; poor intake/dehydration; persistent vomiting; severe or worsening cough; cold extremities or rapid breathing with chest retractions or cyanosis. Prevention includes annual vaccination, hand and respiratory hygiene, avoiding touching eyes/nose/mouth, covering coughs, clean environment, and avoiding self-medication with antivirals or antibiotics. In Vietnam, a 4-year-old girl developed seizures and coma two days after fever and upper respiratory symptoms; throat swab was positive for Influenza A and she was diagnosed with Acute Necrotizing Encephalopathy (ANE) related to influenza A after transfer to the National Children's Hospital, receiving intensive treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Population aging poses the challenge of protecting the elderly against infectious diseases.
article.articleSummary: Vietnam’s aging population, combined with immune senescence and chronic diseases, increases vulnerability to infections among older adults. RSV is highlighted as a key threat: a five-year model projects 4.6 million RSV-related acute respiratory infections among people aged 60 and older, with 200,000 hospitalizations and 18,000 deaths from RSV-related lower respiratory infections. The risk is higher for those with COPD, cardiovascular disease, or other chronic illnesses. Data presented at an RSV in elderly conference organized by the Vietnamese Gerontology Association in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City underscores the burden. International guidelines from GOLD and the US CDC stress vaccination to protect high-risk elderly. In practice at Bach Mai Hospital and the Institute of Tropical Medicine, vaccination counseling is integrated into routine care, with clinicians reviewing history and tailoring vaccines (influenza annually, pneumococcus, herpes zoster, RSV) by age. Influenza and shingles add to the burden, reinforcing immunization to prevent severe outcomes.

article.articleHeadline: Fever and vomiting in a 1-month-old baby; septic shock and multi-organ failure in critical condition.
article.articleSummary: On 14 September 2026, a 50‑day‑old infant from A Dơi commune, Quảng Trị Province, Vietnam, presented with fever, vomiting and frequent diarrhea, progressing to septic shock and multi‑organ failure due to a gastrointestinal infection. Dehydrated and in shock on transfer from Huong Hoa General Hospital to Quang Tri General Hospital, the child developed acute respiratory distress, liver and kidney dysfunction, electrolyte disturbances and coagulopathy. An urgent pediatric intensive care response included endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors and early antibiotics, with 24/7 monitoring of vitals, urine output and labs. After aggressive resuscitation, infection was controlled and organ functions gradually recovered; vasopressors were tapered and the infant breathed spontaneously. After two weeks of treatment, the child was fully recovered with no sequelae and discharged. The report urges prompt medical evaluation for febrile, vomiting or diarrheal symptoms in infants under 3 months.

article.articleHeadline: Văn Bàn strengthens disease prevention and control in cattle and poultry herds.
article.articleSummary: On September 13, in Nam Bó hamlet, Văn Bàn Commune's Center for General Services distributed disinfectants and lime powder to support over 90 farming households to disinfect and sanitize cattle and poultry facilities amid ongoing African swine fever (ASF) cases and emerging bovine lumpy skin disease (LSD). A total of 32 liters of disinfectants and 390 kg of lime powder were allocated; each household received 4 kg of lime powder and chemicals to mix per instructions. Households promptly spread lime and spray disinfectants at barns, entrances, and high-risk areas. In addition to sanitation, authorities intensified outreach, urging farmers to monitor livestock health and report unusual signs to authorities. For LSD in cattle, farmers were advised to boost barn hygiene, control insect vectors, and follow expert guidelines. These measures aim to curb spread, protect livestock, minimize losses, and stabilize production in Văn Bàn.

article.articleHeadline: Zambia reports anthrax outbreak, Dozens of animals and people affected
article.articleSummary: Zambia reports suspected anthrax outbreak under investigation in Nabwalya Chiefdom, Mpika District, centered on the Munyamadzi Game Management Area and Munyamadzi River area. Since July 2026, authorities have recorded deaths of 46 hippopotamuses, 5 buffaloes, 1 crocodile and 8 elephants. About a dozen human cases displaying signs consistent with anthrax have been reported in Nabwalya, linked to consumption of meat from animals found dead in the Munyamadzi River area. The outbreak source and full geographic extent are not yet established; comprehensive surveillance and laboratory investigations are ongoing. Reports of illegal mining around Mukungule are being investigated for potential impacts on rivers, water quality, habitat and wildlife; no causal link to the suspected outbreak has been established. Public advised not to touch, transport, sell or consume animals found dead; unexplained animal deaths should be reported to authorities.

article.articleHeadline: Zambia : Anthrax Outbreak In Mpika
article.articleSummary: Anthrax outbreak in the Nabwalya area of Mpika District, Muchinga Province, Zambia, with confirmed cases in both animals and humans. About 14 human patients are currently receiving treatment; their condition is stable and responding to therapy. More than 26 wild animals have died from anthrax in the affected area, and authorities are intensifying surveillance and restricting movement and consumption of wild meat to curb spread. Government measures include heightened disease surveillance, community sensitisation, and disposal of infected carcasses; the Ministry of Health, with the Disaster Risk Management Division, is supplying medicines to nearby health centres and distributing information materials about anthrax to local communities. Department of National Parks and Wildlife, with security agencies, is restricting wild meat handling to prevent transmission. The pathogen is Bacillus anthracis; humans can become infected from animals or contaminated meat.

article.articleHeadline: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 17 (31 August to 6 September 2026)
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease (BVD) outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is ongoing, with Situation Report No. 17 covering Aug 31–Sept 6, 2026. As of Sept 1, 2026, over 6,200 confirmed BVD cases and more than 3,000 deaths have been reported. Ituri and North Kivu remain heavily affected; ongoing transmission is reported in Haut-Uélé and Bas-Uélé near the CAR border, signaling cross-border risk to Uganda, Tanzania and other countries. The response includes mass health screenings (30,560,048 at points of entry/points of control), support to 230 PoEs/PoCs, and RCCE reach to 26,500,916 individuals. More than 50 IOM-managed IDP sites in Ituri and North Kivu are impacted by the outbreak amid WASH, health, and shelter vulnerabilities. 171 fatalities have been intercepted at PoCs. Preparedness and IPC, border surveillance, and pre-positioning are emphasized for cross-border protection, with Priority 1a (DRC, Uganda) and 1b (Burundi, Rwanda, South Sudan) and Priority 2 (Angola, CAR, Ethiopia, Kenya, Republic of the Congo, Tanzania, Zambia) in focus.

triage.headline_ja: IOM:複数国にまたがるブンディブギョ・エボラウイルス病アウトブレイク - 状況報告書 No.17（2026年8月31日〜9月6日）

triage.notes: 記事はDRC（イトゥリ州、北キブ州、オー・ウエレ州、バ・ウエレ州）での実際の発生を報告。ウガンダ、タンザニア、ザンビア等は越境リスクへの備え・優先国リスト（Priority 1b/2）として言及されているのみで、実際の症例発生地ではないためverified_locationsから除外した。
